newsitem.title: USA: Mexico not intervened for peso this year - Mancera.
newsitem.headline: Mexico not intervened for peso this year - Mancera.

text.p: Mexico stands by its floating exchange rate system, and has not intervened in the markets to support the peso this year, aside from a pre-set August auction, Mexico's central bank head said Saturday.
Miguel Mancera, governor of the Bank of Mexico, also said he saw no reason to devalue the peso, and explained that the currency market should determine its value.

"We are in a floating exchange rate regime so the exchange rate is market-determined," Mancera told reporters. "We have not intervened the whole year, except since August in order to buy dollars according to a program that we announced."
In August, Mexico implemented a program to build dollar reserves that would not affect the market value of the peso.

Mancera, after speaking at the Inter-American Development Bank, said that the net international reserves of the Bank of Mexico have grown by about $4 billion because of government borrowings abroad and revenues from state oil company Pemex, which have increased as the price of oil has risen.
"Pemex sells the foreign exchange they get from exports to the Bank of Mexico," Mancera said. "This is something that has been done and continues to be done."
The governor said that current levels of reserves were sufficient to service its debt requirements and imports.
The Mexican government has not announced its projections for next year, but Mancera said he hoped for higher growth and diminished inflation.
"My expectation is that growth may be somewhere between four and five percent and I would like to see inflation about half of 1996 inflation," Mancera said.

The Mexican government estimates that the cost of cleaning up the banking sector would amount to eight percent of GDP spread over a number of years, but the disbursals up to now have been small, Mancera said.
He also said he thought the banking sector was out of danger.
Mexico will likely prepay some of the borrowing from the U.S. Treasury Department and the International Monetary Fund as part of the country's 1995 rescue package, he said.
"It is something that is likely," Mancera said. "I cannot give you a specific date or amount, but it is something that we would like to do if possible."
The governor defended the transparency of the central bank as evidenced by the weekly publication of the Bank of Mexico's balance sheet and the daily data on the monetary base.
"The market has a very easy way to monitor that we are complying with the program," Mancera said. "I simply cannot see how we could do more. We publish everything."
